newsitem.title: CANADA: Arakis says deal raised interest in Sudan.
newsitem.headline: Arakis says deal raised interest in Sudan.

text.p: Arakis Energy Corp's US$1 billion joint venture deal to develop an oil concession in Sudan has enticed other international energy firms to negotiate for adjacent blocks, Arakis chief executive John McLeod said on Thursday.
McLeod said he was confident that talks were taking place between the Sudanese government and oil companies that were interested in joining the Arakis consortium but did not make the final cut.
"I'm sure they are," he said in an interview.

McLeod has said about 10 companies had tried to negotiate their way into the group, which eventually comprised Arakis, Malaysia state oil company Petronas, China National Petroleum Corp and the Khartoum government.
The consortium was formed to develop the Heglig and Unity fields, which are estimated to harbor 600 million barrels of oil, and build a 950-mile pipeline to the Red Sea from southern Sudan.
"A lot of people who said, 'Well, we can't get into this,' are now turning around and saying, 'Gee, maybe we should get into a block next door,'" he said.
Several sources who have closely watched the Arakis saga, have said Block 5 southeast of the Arakis concession had emerged as a much-desired exploration area.
Like Heglig and Unity, Block 5 was part of the Sudan concession previously owned by Chevron Corp.
"There were some people at Chevron who thought that the really big reserves were southeast of us, but there's only been one well, one (stratographic) test, drilled down there," McLeod said.
He said Occidental Petroleum Corp, which was not part of the final Arakis consortium, was likely keen on alternative Sudan exploration lands.
"They and other companies like them," he said.

Arakis said in announcing its deal last week that U.S.-Sudan diplomatic tensions, which culminated in a U.S. move denying visas to Sudanese officials, closed the door on a U.S. company becoming a consortium member.

Analysts have said new operators in Sudan would add credibility to Arakis' project by providing other sources of production for the US$650 million pipeline, which would then become more of a common carrier.

Meanwhile, McLeod and other Arakis executives were scheduled to meet with several of the company's institutional investors in New York, Boston and Toronto next week to brief them on the status of the project.
The company's shares on Nasdaq were up 3/16 to 4-3/4 on Thursday on just more than a million shares.
